core: The working definition of the general ledger: the complete set of a company's accounts, where every transaction ends up collected by account — attributed to OpenStax's Principles of Accounting
Accounts in the ledger: each asset, liability, equity, revenue, and expense a business uses has its own account — the five families, stated simply; each family has its own sibling topic
Posting named: the step that copies journal entries into the ledger — one line; journal-entries is a sibling topic, referenced only
The ledger's shape: entries recorded chronologically in the journal are sorted by account, and each account's entries accumulate into a running balance — described in words
Why the ledger matters: it turns a diary of events into usable totals — the core value
The chart of accounts: the organized list of every account a business uses — named, with one line
The honest framing: the ledger is the memory of the business — every number on the financial statements traces back to it
supporting: The journal as the chronological record that posting draws from (context; journal mechanics are sibling-owned)
Account numbering in the chart of accounts: assets start with 1, liabilities with 2, equity with 3, revenues with 4, expenses with 5 (one line)
The trial balance is built from the ledger's account balances (sibling topic trial-balance, referenced only)
Ledger accuracy is checked by a trial balance, which confirms total debits equal total credits (sibling topic debits-and-credits, referenced only)

claims.claim: The general ledger is the complete set of a company's accounts, where all transactions are collected by account; OpenStax's Principles of Accounting presents accounts and the general ledger as the basic components of even the simplest accounting system.

Each asset, liability, equity, revenue, and expense a business uses has its own account in the ledger; the five families are tracked separately, and every account a company maintains lives in its general ledger.
Posting is the step that moves journal entries into the general ledger: it takes all transactions recorded in the journal during a period and transfers the information to the ledger.
The ledger is organized by account rather than by date: every account used during the period appears there, and each account accumulates its own entries so its balance can be read directly.

The general ledger is the primary source for the trial balance and the financial statements: it is the data source used to construct the balance sheet and the income statement, so it turns a diary of events into usable totals.

The chart of accounts is the organized, numbered list of every account a business uses, presented in the order the accounts appear on the financial statements — balance sheet accounts first, then income statement accounts.
The ledger records all past transactions of a company organized by account, so it functions as the memory of the business: every figure on the statements traces back to it.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Whether the general ledger is a physical book, a software file, or a report. Textbooks describe it as a record of accounts; accounting software presents it as a live, sortable file; CFI calls it a record of all past transactions organized by accounts.
positions: A ledger is a bound book of accounts (traditional view)
A ledger is any organized collection of accounts, paper or electronic (functional view)
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson teaches the functional view: the ledger is the complete set of accounts, whether kept in a paper book or in accounting software. The form changes; the job does not.

conflictingEvidence.issue: How many account families exist. OpenStax discusses accounts within assets, liabilities, and equity in the expanded equation, while CFI lists assets, liabilities, equity, revenue, and expenses as the accounting elements a ledger tracks.
positions: Three families in the accounting equation: assets, liabilities, equity
Five families tracked as accounts: assets, liabilities, equity, revenue, expenses
conflictingEvidence.resolution: Both sources agree on the same five families as accounts; the three-way split is the equation view and the five-way split is the account view. The lesson uses the five families, stated simply, and notes that each family has its own sibling topic.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Whether posting happens by hand, entry by entry, or automatically in software. Older descriptions emphasize manual copying from journal to ledger; modern accounting software posts entries to the ledger automatically as they are saved.
positions: Posting is a manual copying step performed by a bookkeeper
Software posts entries to ledger accounts automatically
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson names posting as the step that transfers journal entries into the ledger and notes that in software it happens automatically; the concept is the same either way.
